newsitem.title: USA: Dollar tops fresh hurdles against yen, mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar tops fresh hurdles against yen, mark.

text.p: The dollar surged to its highest level against the Japanese yen in almost four years on Tuesday, buoyed by evidence that the world's major industrial nations remain content with the dollar's current strength.

The dollar rose to its highest level in more than two and a half years against the German mark and the Swiss franc, after a benign report on U.S. labour costs soothed fears of inflation and fuelled early gains in the stock and bond markets.
The dollar began rising overseas after a Japanese finance official indicated that the yen's recent slide against the dollar was not a cause for immediate concern.
Gains were reinforced when Juergen Stark of the German finance ministry referred to dollar gains against the mark as a "normalization" of imbalances between the two currencies.

These comments were a signal to many in the market that, despite its sharp recent rise, support for a strong dollar remains firm. In the absence of any dollar-negative statements on Tuesday, the dollar continued its climb against the yen.
"Nobody talked the dollar down so it had only one way to move," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer.

The dollar got a further boost after the Labour Department reported that its employment cost index, a measure of wage and benefit costs, rose by 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, less than Wall Street economists had anticipated.
The bond market welcomed the news as a sign that wage-driven inflation was under control, jumping sharply after the release of the numbers, and creating a ripple effect in U.S. stocks and the dollar.
But late profit-taking in the stock and bond markets pushed the dollar off its highs late in the day.
The dollar ended the day at 120.95 yen, up from 119.57 late Monday. It reached a peak of 121.77 yen during the session, its highest level since February 1993.
Against the mark, the dollar retreated from sharp early gains to close little changed at 1.6470 vs. 1.6473 late Monday. Early Tuesday it reached a high of 1.6570 marks, its top level since June 1994.
"The dollar was really tied to the bonds and stocks," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers & Traders Bank.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended the day down 4.61 points at 6,656.08 after rising as much as 100 points earlier.

After rising well over a point earlier, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended up 7/32, or $2.19 on a $1,000 bond, reducing its yield to 6.93 percent from 6.94 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Rumours surfaced that the Federal Reserve was monitoring exchange rate fluctuations on behalf of the Bank of Japan, but they did little to stem the dollar's rise against the yen.
By contrast, talk last Friday that the Bank of Japan was selling dollars to defend the yen toppled the dollar from its highs against the Japanese currency.

"I think they're concerned about the pace but not necessarily the level," said Doug Lee, corporate foreign exchange dealer at Sakura Bank Ltd, referring to the Group of Seven industrial nations. "They want to make sure the pace is stabilised and that it doesn't go up too fast too soon which it has recently."
In other trade, the dollar ended slightly weaker at 1.4270 Swiss francs against 1.4303 late Monday. The British pound fell to $1.6190 against $1.6220.
The dollar fell modestly to Canadian $1.3402 from C$1.3440.
